newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Supply no sweat in Europe but US wary.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Supply no sweat in Europe but US wary.

text.p: Expectations of interest rate cuts in Europe have provided an optimistic tone for a swathe of recent bond issues, analysts said on Wednesday.
But in the U.S., the forthcoming quarterly refunding may be overshadowed by the threat that the Federal Reserve will be forced to raise interest rates.

"Supply in the U.S. is more of a problem than in Europe," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "There, the market has a rush of corporate issues, the new index-linked 10-year, as well as the refunding."
The U.S. Treasury holds its first sale of index-linked debt later this session, some $7.0 billion of 10-year notes.
Analysts said there were concerns that the Fed will hike interest rates, if not as early as a February 4 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, then at least in the first half.

Brian Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, said the U.S. may need to get the rate hike out of the way in order to remove the uncertainty overhanging the market and to restore flagging confidence.
In Europe however, expectations of a cut in German interest rates are still being fostered by the market. And if Germany were to cut, others could follow.
Germany's top-up Bund auction on Tuesday met a positive reaction, analysts said. Roberts noted that the auction had also been increased to 12 billion marks from an expected 10 billion.

"At the moment the Bundesbank is content to see a weak mark and a fall in debt yields, but they may be persuaded to cut by the end of the first quarter," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"France could even cut independently, although given their natural caution, they may want to wait until after the Bundesbank," he said.
Italy was also a candidate for rate cutting, he said.
Even though Britain is unlikely to see a reduction in interest rates, expectations of a rise ahead of the election, which must be held by May 22, have dwindled.
Investors queued up to buy gilts at Tuesday's auction, with demand for the 10-year bonds more than double the 2.5 billion stg of debt on offer.
"Gilts have been the poor man of Europe for so long, that now when the spread opens up, people are prepared to snap it up," said Roberts.
A further 1.5 billion stg of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002 is expected on Thursday.

Stamenkovic said the gilt auction was likely to go well, as the fiscal position in Britain was far more favourable than in Spain or Italy, whose debt assets are currently outperforming those of Britain.
Benchmark 10-year gilts have a yield spread of 181 basis points over comparable Bunds, while the Italian BTP/Bund spread is 141 basis points and the Spanish Bonos/Bund spread is 90 basis points.

Analysts said, however, that there was a chance that weakness in Treasuries could bleed through into the European bond complex, despite the degree of divergence which the market has recently experienced.
The overnight fall in Treasuries on the back of inflation worries, for example, led to a weaker tone across European bonds.

"If the U.S. hikes rates, it may be very hard to persuade investors to buy bonds or equities anywhere," said Venables. "Investors seem to synchronised in a way that is unjustified from a theoretical point of view."
